claim: Parameter-based knowledge editing cannot reliably update factual knowledge in a large language model without damaging its core capabilities. The near-perfect editing results reported in prior work do not survive realistic evaluation, and the limitation is geometric rather than incidental: localized weight edits are disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model's representation space and propagate globally, so damage compounds as edits accumulate. A parameter-free approach that leaves the weights untouched is therefore a serious alternative to parameter editing rather than a fallback.
subclaims: Can parameter-based knowledge editing reliably update factual knowledge in a large language model without damaging its core capabilities?
Do the near-perfect editing results reported in prior work survive realistic evaluation?
Is the limitation of parameter-based knowledge editing geometric rather than incidental?
Are localized weight edits disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model's representation space?
Do localized weight edits propagate globally?
Does damage compound as edits accumulate?
Does a parameter-free approach leave the model weights untouched?
Is a parameter-free approach a serious alternative to parameter editing rather than a fallback?

experiments: To address subclaim 1, 2, and 6, run a controlled multi-edit benchmark comparing parameter-based knowledge editing methods against an unedited baseline and a parameter-free alternative on realistic evaluation suites. Use a public causal LLM that can be edited locally (for example GPT-J or LLaMA-2-7B if licensing permits) and public knowledge-editing benchmarks such as CounterFact, MultiCounterFact, zsRE, and RippleEdits, supplemented with broader capability checks from MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC, TruthfulQA, and perplexity on WikiText-103 or The Pile validation split. Evaluate several parameter-editing methods from prior work (for example ROME, MEMIT, MEND) under both single-edit and sequential-edit settings with edit counts increasing across a schedule such as 1, 10, 100, 500. For each stage, measure: edit success on paraphrases, robustness to rephrasings, specificity vs unintended spillover, downstream task performance, calibration, and generation quality under realistic prompts rather than only templated probes. Compare these results to a parameter-free method that applies retrieval, external memory, or in-context patching without changing weights. If parameter-editing methods maintain high edit success while preserving downstream scores and specificity even after many edits, the main claim is weakened. If apparent near-perfect performance on narrow probes degrades substantially under paraphrases, broader tasks, or edit accumulation while the parameter-free approach preserves core capabilities, that supports the claim that prior results do not survive realistic evaluation and that damage compounds. This experiment could become less necessary if there already exists a public, methodologically strong benchmark paper evaluating the same methods on multi-edit, paraphrase-robust, broad-capability suites with released code and models.

To address subclaim 3, 4, and 5, perform a mechanistic geometry study of localized weight edits and their propagation through representation space. Start with a public transformer and a parameter-editing method that applies localized updates to specific MLP or attention weights. On a large public text corpus such as WikiText-103, The Pile subsets, or C4, collect hidden-state activations at layers implicated by the editor and estimate the local covariance eigenspectrum of those representations. For each applied edit, decompose the induced change in hidden activations and logits into components aligned with high-variance versus low-variance eigen-directions of the pre-edit representation space. Then quantify whether the edit produces disproportionately large functional changes per unit perturbation along low-variance directions, and trace propagation by measuring activation/logit shifts on a broad unrelated prompt set across layers and tokens. Add controls: random weight perturbations with matched norm, edits projected onto high-variance subspaces, and edits constrained to be orthogonal to low-variance directions. If true factual edits consistently show amplification along low-variance directions and broader prompt-wise propagation than matched random perturbations, that supports a geometric limitation rather than an incidental one. If constrained edits that avoid low-variance directions reduce collateral damage while preserving edit success, that strongly supports the proposed mechanism. If no such directional amplification or global propagation is observed, the geometric claim is weakened. This experiment could be made less necessary by existing public mechanistic analyses that already show eigenspace-resolved amplification and propagation with strong causal controls across multiple editing methods.

To address subclaim 7 and 8, compare a weight-preserving parameter-free system against parameter-editing systems in an end-to-end factual update setting that values reversibility, auditability, and preserved base-model competence. Implement a parameter-free approach using public retrieval components or external memory over an editable fact store built from public datasets such as Wikidata-derived triples, Natural Questions, FEVER, and CounterFact facts; verify cryptographically or by exact checkpoint hashing that model weights remain unchanged before and after updates. Then test the system against parameter-edited models on realistic tasks requiring both updated facts and ordinary reasoning: direct factual QA, multi-hop questions, contradiction detection, and long-form generation with citations or provenance. Measure update latency, rollback ability, edit precision, dependence on retrieval quality, downstream task retention, and performance under conflicting or temporally changing facts. If the parameter-free method achieves competitive factual update accuracy while preserving base capabilities, enabling easy rollback and leaving weights untouched, that supports it as a serious alternative rather than merely a fallback. If it only works in narrow retrieval-friendly settings and underperforms badly on integrated generation or reasoning, the claim is weaker. This experiment could be less necessary if there is already a public benchmark with released systems showing comparable or superior end-to-end factual update performance for parameter-free methods under equal compute and context budgets.

To address subclaim 1 and subclaim 2, run a realistic end-to-end benchmark comparing parameter-based editors against a parameter-free alternative on broad post-edit utility, not just edit success. Use publicly available editing benchmarks such as MQuAKE, UniEdit, and CounterFact/ZsRE if available via HuggingFace or the corresponding paper repositories, and evaluate on an open-weight model family such as Llama-2/3-7B or Mistral-7B. Implement several parameter-editing methods commonly reported as strong baselines (for example ROME, MEMIT, MEND, FT) and at least one parameter-free method that leaves base weights unchanged, such as retrieval-augmented generation over an external fact store or an inference-time adapter/context injection method with frozen weights. For each requested fact update, measure: edit success on direct prompts; paraphrase generalization; locality on unrelated prompts; multi-hop/ripple consistency using MQuAKE; broad capability retention on held-out tasks unrelated to the edited facts, e.g. MMLU subsets, TruthfulQA, HellaSwag, ARC, GSM8K, and perplexity on WikiText-2 or The Pile validation shard; and performance as the number of sequential edits grows (1, 10, 100, 1000). A key design point is to evaluate under realistic prompting, paraphrases, compositional questions, and subject/relation distribution shift, rather than only the narrow templates used by prior editing papers. If parameter-based methods retain near-perfect direct edit accuracy but degrade substantially on paraphrases, MQuAKE ripple questions, or broad capabilities—especially relative to a parameter-free method—this would support the claim that prior near-perfect results do not survive realistic evaluation and that weight-preserving alternatives are serious contenders. If instead parameter editing remains strong across these broader metrics and scales to many edits with little degradation, the main claim would be weakened. This experiment could become partly unnecessary if a large, independent benchmark study already reports these exact cross-method comparisons under standardized realistic evaluation and multiple edit budgets.

To address subclaim 6, subclaim 5, and part of subclaim 1, perform a controlled accumulation-and-propagation study that isolates whether damage compounds as edits accumulate and whether supposedly localized edits spread globally. Start with a public benchmark of atomic factual edits such as CounterFact or ZsRE and group edits by semantic relatedness using Wikidata relations or entity neighborhoods. On one or more open-weight LLMs, apply edits in batches of increasing size and order: random unrelated edits, semantically clustered edits, and adversarially interfering edits (same relation, overlapping entities, or contradictory neighborhoods). After each batch, evaluate not only edited facts but also: untouched facts sharing the same relation; facts sharing only the subject or object type; distant unrelated facts; hidden-state changes across layers for a fixed public probe set; and downstream task accuracy/perplexity. To test global propagation, compare the geographic “footprint” of an edit by measuring how many unrelated prompts flip answers or logits beyond a threshold, and map representational drift across many tokens and layers before versus after editing. If answer changes and representational drift expand far beyond the targeted neighborhood, and if utility loss rises superlinearly with number of edits—especially for clustered or interfering edits—that would support the claim that damage compounds and that local weight edits propagate globally. If drift remains tightly local and aggregate quality declines only minimally even after many edits, those subclaims would be undermined. This experiment would be less necessary if there were already publicly available large-scale sequential-edit studies reporting both broad downstream performance and layerwise drift maps across edit budgets.

To address subclaim 3 and subclaim 4, test the proposed geometric mechanism directly by relating edit-induced changes to the model’s representation covariance spectrum. Using an open-weight transformer and public corpora such as Wikipedia or C4 for sampling activations, estimate layerwise representation covariance at the token positions and modules targeted by editing methods (for example the key/value spaces or MLP activations used by ROME/MEMIT-style updates). For each applied factual edit from CounterFact or ZsRE, decompose the induced parameter update and the resulting activation/logit perturbations into the eigenbasis of the pre-edit representation covariance. Then quantify whether perturbation energy and downstream behavioral change are disproportionately concentrated in low-variance directions relative to matched random updates, norm-matched high-variance-direction updates, and functionally equivalent constrained edits if such optimization is possible. A stronger causal variant is to construct synthetic edits whose update vectors are explicitly projected onto low-variance versus high-variance subspaces while matching target edit success, then compare collateral damage, propagation footprint, and sequential-edit stability. If low-variance-aligned edits consistently produce larger-than-expected global behavioral changes and more collateral damage at equal direct edit success, that would support the claim that the limitation is geometric rather than incidental and that low-variance directions amplify edits. If no such relationship appears, or if damage is explained better by update norm, layer choice, or relation frequency than by spectral alignment, the geometric hypothesis would be weakened. This experiment could be made less necessary by prior evidence that already publishes eigenspace-resolved analyses of edit perturbations together with causal interventions showing that subspace alignment, not just size or location of the update, predicts collateral damage.

To address subclaim 1 ("Can parameter-based knowledge editing reliably update factual knowledge in a large language model without damaging its core capabilities?") and subclaims 2, 6, and 8, run a realistic sequential-edit benchmark comparing parameter-editing methods (ROME, MEMIT or MEND if available, plus small-step fine-tuning / constrained fine-tuning) against parameter-free or parameter-preserving alternatives (IKE and, if implementable, a retrieval/memory editor) on GPT-2 and GPT-J. Use public COUNTERFACT and ZSRE edit sets, filtering out unrecallable or trivial instances as the field expects. Evaluate edits cumulatively with no rollback at batch sizes / sequence lengths 1, 10, 100, and 1000. After each prefix of edits, measure Reliability on edited prompts, Generalization on paraphrase/equivalent neighborhoods, Locality on out-of-scope prompts, COUNTERFACT ES/PS/NS, and broad capability preservation on public robustness sets such as HellaSwag, LAMBADA, and Natural Questions; also track perplexity/fluency if available. Include the unedited model, in-context editing baseline, and cross-dataset replication on both COUNTERFACT and ZSRE. If parameter editors show good single-edit efficacy but materially worse locality, broader-task performance, or rapid degradation under cumulative edits relative to parameter-free methods, that supports the claim that reliable factual updating without harming core capabilities does not survive realistic evaluation and that parameter-free methods are serious alternatives rather than fallbacks. If instead parameter editors maintain high reliability/generalization with flat locality and downstream-task curves even after many cumulative edits, the core claim is weakened. This experiment would become less necessary if there already existed a public, cross-backbone, no-rollback benchmark showing cumulative edit trajectories together with unrelated capability metrics for both parameter-based and parameter-free methods.

To address subclaim 3 ("Is the limitation of parameter-based knowledge editing geometric rather than incidental?"), subclaim 4 ("Are localized weight edits disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model's representation space?"), and subclaim 5 ("Do localized weight edits propagate globally?"), perform a representation-geometry and intervention analysis around the edited modules. For each edit instance on GPT-2 and GPT-J using ROME/MEND, collect hidden states for a large public text corpus sample (e.g., WikiText-103 via HuggingFace or The Pile subset if compute allows) and estimate layerwise covariance eigenspectra for the residual stream / edited MLP input-output representations. Compute each induced activation change or effective parameter-update-induced output shift, project it onto the principal-component basis, and quantify whether update energy and downstream logit effect are concentrated in low-variance directions more than expected from matched random updates, layer-matched fine-tuning steps, or sham edits. Then test propagation by measuring representational drift and output changes on unrelated prompts across layers/tokens before and after the edit, using both causal tracing and the alternative representation-zeroing procedure to reduce dependence on one localization method. A key control is to compare equal-norm perturbations aligned to high-variance versus low-variance eigendirections and measure locality damage, unrelated-task degradation, and spread across prompts. If low-variance-aligned changes consistently yield larger output effects and more global drift than high-variance or random directions, and real edits are enriched in those directions, that supports a geometric mechanism rather than incidental implementation quirks. If real edits are not preferentially aligned to low-variance directions, or matched perturbations do not differ in amplification/global spread, the geometric explanation is weakened. This experiment could be partly obviated by existing public analyses directly reporting eigenspace projections of real edit updates together with matched-direction intervention controls across multiple backbones.

With respect to evidence piece Y on "Layer and token sweep," "Edit-layer/location sweep," and "Alternative localization procedure," test whether reported near-perfect edit localization/success is largely an artifact of optimistic evaluation choices rather than true robustness. For a shared set of COUNTERFACT and ZSRE facts, run ROME, MEND, and fine-tuning across many candidate layers and subject-token indices instead of only the peak or recommended location. For each configuration, evaluate not just canonical edit prompts but paraphrase neighborhoods, portability probes (subject replace, reversed relation, one-hop or multi-hop where available), and out-of-scope locality sets; repeat localization using both causal tracing with multiple corruption magnitudes and representation zeroing. Fit regressions predicting edit success and collateral damage from layer choice, token choice, localization score, and their interactions to determine whether apparent success is mostly explained by favorable layer selection. If strong results collapse outside narrow layer/token settings, if tracing adds little explanatory power beyond layer identity, or if paraphrase/portability/locality metrics are much worse than canonical efficacy, that supports subclaim 2 that near-perfect results from prior work do not survive realistic evaluation. If success remains high and stable across layers, tokens, localization variants, and stricter probes, the claim is weakened. This experiment would be less necessary if prior papers had already released comprehensive layer-token sweep tables with realistic neighborhood/portability evaluations and showed robustness to alternative localization procedures.

To address subclaim 1, Can parameter-based knowledge editing reliably update factual knowledge in a large language model without damaging its core capabilities?, and subclaim 2, Do the near-perfect editing results reported in prior work survive realistic evaluation?, run a head-to-head evaluation of several parameter-editing methods such as ROME, MEMIT, MEND, and fine-tuning against a parameter-free retrieval or in-context editing baseline. Use public datasets such as CounterFact, zsRE, WikiData5M, and Natural Questions for edit facts, and evaluate not only exact edit success but also paraphrase robustness, neighborhood specificity, inverse/relation-consistency questions, multi-hop implications, and unrelated factual queries. Measure core capability damage on public benchmarks such as MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC, LAMBADA, WinoGrande, TruthfulQA, and perplexity on WikiText-103 or C4 validation subsets. If parameter edits achieve high edit success while preserving paraphrase generalization, locality, consistency, and benchmark performance within confidence intervals of the unedited model, the broad claim is weakened. If exact-prompt success is high but realistic generalization falls, unrelated facts change, or benchmark scores/perplexity degrade, the claim is supported. Include bootstrap confidence intervals and compare damage per successful edit to the parameter-free baseline. This experiment could be made unnecessary if there were already independently replicated results using realistic edit, locality, consistency, and general-capability evaluations across multiple public datasets and editing methods.

To address subclaim 3, Is the limitation of parameter-based knowledge editing geometric rather than incidental?, subclaim 4, Are localized weight edits disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model's representation space?, and subclaim 5, Do localized weight edits propagate globally?, perform a representation-geometry audit before and after editing. For an open model such as GPT-J, Llama-2/3 open-weight variants, or Pythia, compute hidden-state covariance spectra at edited layers using public corpora such as WikiText-103, C4, and CounterFact prompts. Apply ROME or MEMIT edits from CounterFact/zsRE, then decompose edit-induced activation changes into principal-component directions of the pre-edit representation space. Test whether changes have unusually large components in low-variance eigenspaces, whether the Jacobian or logit response amplifies those directions more than high-variance directions, and whether activation/logit perturbations appear on unrelated prompts, layers, tokens, and tasks. Possible results: if edit effects concentrate in low-variance directions and those components predict global output shifts or benchmark degradation, the geometric mechanism is supported; if damage is uncorrelated with representation spectrum and is explained instead by implementation choices, optimization instability, or specific layers, the geometric subclaim is weakened. This experiment could be made unnecessary by prior evidence showing, across models and editors, a causal link between low-variance representation directions, amplified edit effects, and unrelated-behavior changes.

To address subclaim 6, Does damage compound as edits accumulate?, subclaim 7, Does a parameter-free approach leave the model weights untouched?, and subclaim 8, Is a parameter-free approach a serious alternative to parameter editing rather than a fallback?, run a scaling experiment with increasing edit counts, for example 1, 10, 100, 1,000, and 10,000 facts from CounterFact, zsRE, WikiData5M, or Wikidata-derived recent-change sets. After each batch, evaluate edit success, paraphrase generalization, specificity, unrelated factual QA, calibration, perplexity, and general benchmarks, using the same random edit order across methods. Compare parameter editors with a parameter-free method such as retrieval-augmented generation over an edit memory, nearest-neighbor fact lookup, or prompted patching; verify the parameter-free claim by hashing all model weight tensors before and after the run and logging that only the external memory/index changes. If parameter-editing damage grows superlinearly or monotonically while the parameter-free method preserves base benchmark scores and achieves competitive factual update accuracy, the claim that damage compounds and that parameter-free editing is a serious alternative is supported. If parameter editing scales to thousands of edits with stable locality and no capability loss while outperforming parameter-free methods on latency, accuracy, and robustness, the claim is weakened. This experiment could be made unnecessary if large-scale, independently replicated edit-accumulation curves and weight-hash audits already existed for both parameter-based and parameter-free approaches.

To address subclaim "Do the near-perfect editing results reported in prior work survive realistic evaluation?" run a head-to-head reproduction of standard parameter-editing methods such as ROME, MEMIT, MEND, and fine-tuning baselines on public models such as GPT-J-6B or Llama-2-7B, first using the original narrow metrics on CounterFact and zsRE, then using broader public evaluations: MQuAKE for multi-hop ripple effects, RippleEdits or UniEdit for related-fact consistency, and general capability benchmarks such as MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC, GSM8K, TruthfulQA, and WikiText perplexity. Apply single edits and batches of increasing size, e.g. 1, 10, 100, 1,000 edits, and measure edit success, paraphrase/generalization success, locality/specificity, unrelated-prompt behavioral drift, calibration, and benchmark degradation. If prior near-perfect scores persist only on narrow edit-recall metrics but collapse on ripple, paraphrase, unrelated factual queries, or general benchmarks, that would support the claim that earlier evaluations were unrealistic and that parameter editing is not reliably non-destructive. If methods maintain high edit success, ripple consistency, and unchanged general capabilities across realistic tests, the claim is weakened. This experiment could be made partly unnecessary by a sufficiently broad, independently replicated benchmark report that already evaluates the same editing methods under multi-hop, locality, accumulated-edit, and core-capability conditions.

To address subclaim "Is the limitation of parameter-based knowledge editing geometric rather than incidental?" measure how edits interact with the model's representation geometry. For a public model such as GPT-J-6B or Llama-2-7B, collect hidden states over a large public text sample such as WikiText-103 or C4 and compute layerwise covariance eigenspectra. After applying localized edits with ROME or MEMIT on CounterFact or zsRE, decompose the induced hidden-state changes and weight-update effects into high-variance versus low-variance representation directions. Then test whether low-variance components have disproportionately large downstream logit effects, whether perturbations matched for norm but placed in low-variance directions cause more global behavioral drift than high-variance perturbations, and whether the same phenomenon appears across layers and unrelated prompts. If edit-induced changes concentrate in or are amplified through low-variance directions and these components predict unrelated-output drift better than edit norm or layer alone, that would support the geometric mechanism claimed. If damage is instead explained by simple factors such as excessive update norm, bad hyperparameters, edit-data artifacts, or particular algorithms, the geometric subclaim is weakened. This experiment could be made unnecessary by direct mechanistic evidence from prior work showing eigenspace-resolved amplification and causal intervention tests for knowledge-edit updates.

To address subclaim "Is a parameter-free approach a serious alternative to parameter editing rather than a fallback?" compare a parameter-free update system against parameter-editing baselines under the same edit workload. Implement retrieval-augmented generation or an external edit-memory method using a public corpus/index, e.g. Wikipedia passages from HuggingFace datasets, edited triples from CounterFact/zsRE/UniEdit, and MQuAKE questions for ripple evaluation. Verify that model weights are unchanged using parameter checksums before and after inference, then evaluate edit accuracy, paraphrase generalization, multi-hop consistency, unrelated-query locality, core benchmarks such as MMLU/HellaSwag/GSM8K, latency, context-length cost, and robustness to conflicting or stale retrieved evidence. If the parameter-free system preserves core capabilities while matching or exceeding parameter-editing methods on factual-update success and ripple consistency, especially as edits accumulate, it supports the claim that parameter-free methods are serious alternatives. If it fails on latency, retrieval brittleness, multi-hop reasoning, adversarial phrasing, or cannot generalize beyond explicit stored facts while parameter editing succeeds without damage, the claim is weakened. This experiment could be made less necessary by strong published comparisons showing parameter-free and parameter-editing systems evaluated on identical edit sets, ripple effects, accumulated updates, and general-capability preservation.

To address subclaim 1, run a realistic cumulative-edit benchmark comparing parameter-based editors against the unedited model and a parameter-free baseline. Use public COUNTERFACT and ZSRE edit sets with GPT-J and GPT-2-XL or another openly available HuggingFace backbone, and apply ROME, MEMIT/MEND where available, constrained fine-tuning, and an in-context or retrieval-based method such as IKE/SERAC-style inference-time editing. Filter to examples the base model can answer, then perform sequential no-rollback edits at batch sizes 1, 10, 100, and 1000. After each edit block, measure Reliability on edited prompts, Generalization/Paraphrase Score on equivalent prompts, Locality/Neighborhood Score on out-of-scope prompts, and unrelated capability damage on HellaSwag, LAMBADA, and Natural Questions perplexity or accuracy. If parameter editors preserve high Reliability and Generalization while maintaining locality and unrelated-task performance as edits accumulate, the claim that they cannot reliably update knowledge without damage is weakened. If edit success remains high only for isolated rollback edits but locality, perplexity, or downstream task accuracy degrades cumulatively, the claim is supported. This experiment could be made less necessary by existing public sequential-edit logs across the same models, editors, edit counts, and unrelated capability tasks rather than only single-edit aggregate scores.

With respect to evidence piece COUNTERFACT evaluation suite, replicate the near-perfect editing results under increasingly realistic evaluation variants. On COUNTERFACT and ZSRE, reproduce the original ES/PS/NS aggregate scores for ROME, MEMIT, and MEND under their standard single-edit rollback protocol, then re-score the same edits using stricter paraphrase sets, semantically checked neighborhood prompts, portability probes such as subject-replace/reversed/one-hop questions, MQuAKE-style multi-hop questions if available, and held-out unrelated prompts. Include pre-edit, fine-tuning, and in-context baselines, and report not only aggregate Score S but the full Reliability, Generalization, Locality, Fluency, Consistency, and mean-rank/perplexity changes. If near-perfect scores persist across paraphrases, portability, multi-hop propagation, and unrelated capabilities, the subclaim that prior results fail realistic evaluation is weakened. If scores collapse outside canonical prompts or are accompanied by locality and fluency degradation, it supports the claim that prior results are evaluation-fragile. This experiment could be made unnecessary by audited benchmark releases that already include validated paraphrases, nontrivial portability probes, human-checked prompts, and non-rollback evaluation for the same prior methods.

To address subclaim 4, directly test the proposed geometric mechanism by measuring whether localized weight edits are amplified along low-variance representation directions and whether that predicts global propagation and compounded damage. For each edited fact in COUNTERFACT or ZSRE, collect hidden states from a large public text sample such as WikiText-103 or C4 validation prompts, estimate each edited layer’s representation covariance spectrum, decompose the pre/post-edit activation change induced by ROME/MEMIT/MEND into principal-component directions, and compute amplification as change magnitude divided by the baseline variance along each direction. Then evaluate whether low-variance-direction amplification predicts changes on unrelated prompts, locality failures, perplexity increases, and degradation after 10/100/1000 sequential edits, controlling for layer, edit norm, relation type, and baseline fact confidence. Replicate with representation zeroing or causal tracing to separate geometry from a tracing artifact. If damage and global propagation are strongly predicted by low-variance amplification even after controls, the geometric limitation hypothesis is supported. If edit damage is explained mainly by edit size, layer choice, implementation, or dataset relation, and low-variance directions add little explanatory power, the geometric subclaim is weakened. This experiment could be made unnecessary by released activation-difference/covariance analyses showing the same low-variance amplification pattern across models, editors, and datasets.

To address subclaims 1, 2, and 6, run a preregistered sequential-edit evaluation of parameter-based methods such as ROME, MEMIT, and fine-tuning on publicly available EleutherAI GPT-J-6B or GPT-NeoX models. Draw factual updates from the Hugging Face CounterFact and zsRE datasets, separating subjects and relations across train and test sets. Apply 1, 10, 100, and 1,000 edits, in multiple randomized orders and seeds, and evaluate edit success on the original prompt, paraphrase generalization, multi-hop or portability questions, unrelated-neighbor specificity, and reversion to the old fact. Before and after every edit batch, measure core capabilities using public benchmarks such as WikiText-103 perplexity, MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC, and TruthfulQA; also measure output-distribution KL divergence on a fixed, unrelated prompt set. Compare results with an unedited model, sham updates matched for weight-change norm, and ordinary continued fine-tuning. Report confidence intervals and the fraction of runs satisfying a preregistered joint criterion for successful updating, locality, and capability retention rather than reporting edit efficacy alone. High single-prompt success accompanied by poor paraphrase transfer, unrelated behavioral changes, benchmark degradation, or degradation that grows superlinearly with edit count would support the claim that near-perfect results do not survive realistic evaluation and that damage compounds. Stable efficacy, locality, and capability across seeds and large edit batches would weaken those subclaims. This experiment could be unnecessary if prior work supplied reproducible checkpoints and the same longitudinal, multi-metric evaluation with adequate seeds and controls.

To address subclaims 3, 4, and 5, perform a causal representation-geometry study on the same models and edits. Estimate layerwise activation covariances from a public corpus such as WikiText-103 or a public C4 subset, then eigendecompose or randomized-SVD the covariance matrices to identify low- and high-variance representation directions. For every localized weight edit, measure the edit-induced activation displacement projected onto each variance band, normalized by edit norm, and trace that displacement through later layers and across thousands of unrelated prompts from WikiText-103, CounterFact, and zsRE. Test causality by constructing equal-Frobenius-norm controls: project the update away from low-variance directions, concentrate it into those directions, randomly rotate it, and use sham updates matched for layer, rank, and norm. Re-evaluate factual efficacy, output KL divergence, unrelated-token changes, benchmark performance, and downstream-layer amplification. Repeat across layers, editing methods, facts, and random seeds, and use mediation or regression analyses to test whether low-variance alignment predicts global damage beyond update norm and edit difficulty. Disproportionate amplification and broader propagation for low-variance-aligned updates, together with reduced damage after removing those components, would provide causal evidence for a geometric limitation; equal effects across variance bands or effects explained by update magnitude, optimizer choice, or specific layers would favor an incidental implementation explanation. Public release of activation statistics, edit deltas, and equivalent causal projection tests from multiple model families could substitute for rerunning this experiment.

To address subclaims 7 and 8, compare the strongest parameter editor from experiment 1 with a parameter-free retrieval-and-context system on identical factual-update streams. Use CounterFact and zsRE updates, store each new fact in an external index, retrieve it with a public dense retriever or BM25, and provide the retrieved evidence in the prompt without changing model parameters; include both oracle retrieval and realistic retrieval so retrieval failures are distinguishable from generation failures. Verify that serialized model-weight hashes are identical before and after all updates, while separately recording changes to the external index and prompts. At 1, 10, 100, 1,000, and, if feasible, 10,000 updates, compare factual accuracy, paraphrase generalization, contradiction handling, locality, old-fact suppression, MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC performance, latency, token cost, storage, and robustness when relevant and distractor passages coexist. Include no-update, prompt-only, random-retrieval, and matched-context controls, and evaluate both methods with and without access to their update store to make operational assumptions explicit. If retrieval preserves baseline capabilities while matching or approaching editing accuracy and scaling more safely, it is a serious alternative rather than merely a fallback; if it succeeds only with oracle retrieval, excessive context, or much higher cost, while parameter editing remains accurate and local, that conclusion would be weakened. Unchanged weight hashes establish the narrow weights-untouched claim, but not practical competitiveness. Existing reproducible head-to-head results under the same models, data, resource budgets, and non-oracle retrieval conditions could make this experiment unnecessary.

To address subclaims 1 and 2—whether parameter-based editing reliably updates facts without damaging core capabilities and whether near-perfect results survive realistic evaluation—run a preregistered, seed-controlled comparison of ROME, MEMIT, MEND, and constrained fine-tuning on the publicly available GPT-J-6B model. Draw edits from public CounterFact and zsRE datasets, with MQuAKE, RippleEdits, and UniEdit used to test paraphrases, entailments, multi-hop consequences, temporal consistency, and unrelated-neighborhood locality. Evaluate edit success, paraphrase generalization, logically required ripple updates, contradiction rate, and output-distribution KL divergence on unrelated prompts. Measure core capabilities before and after editing using public WikiText-103 perplexity and Hugging Face versions of MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC, and TruthfulQA. Include unedited-model, sham-edit, and equal-compute fine-tuning controls; use several random seeds and bootstrap confidence intervals rather than reporting only mean success. Near-perfect direct recall accompanied by poor ripple consistency, elevated unrelated KL, or statistically meaningful capability loss would support the claim that conventional evaluations overstate reliability; strong performance across all metrics would weaken it. Complete public per-prompt outputs and checkpoints covering these methods and benchmarks could reduce the need to rerun some baselines, but not the controlled cross-method comparison.

To address subclaims 3–5—whether the limitation is geometric, whether edits are amplified along low-variance representation directions, and whether localized edits propagate globally—instrument the same model and edits from Experiment 1. Estimate layerwise activation covariance from a public, fixed sample of C4 or WikiText-103, eigendecompose each edited layer’s representation space, and project both edit-induced activation changes and the relevant weight-update effects onto covariance eigenvectors. Test whether amplification, defined as output-logit or hidden-state change per unit projected weight change, increases as activation variance decreases. Measure global propagation through layerwise hidden-state divergence and next-token KL on thousands of unrelated C4 prompts. Establish causality with matched controls that preserve update norm, rank, layer, and direct edit success while rotating updates toward low-variance versus high-variance eigenspaces; additionally project the original update away from low-variance directions and retest efficacy and collateral damage. A reproducible inverse variance–amplification relationship, stronger unrelated drift for low-variance-aligned edits, and reduced damage after removing those components would support a geometric mechanism; no relationship after matched controls, or effects explained by update norm or layer alone, would favor an incidental explanation. This experiment could be partly obviated by released activations, exact edit deltas, and covariance spectra, although the causal rotation and projection controls would still be important.

To address subclaims 6–8—whether damage compounds with accumulated edits and whether a weight-preserving method is a serious alternative—apply 1, 10, 50, 100, 500, and, if computationally feasible, 1,000 sequential edits sampled from public CounterFact, MQuAKE, and UniEdit, repeating multiple randomized edit orders. Compare the strongest parameter editor from Experiment 1 with a parameter-free retrieval-augmented baseline that stores the same edited facts in an external FAISS index and injects retrieved evidence into the prompt. Verify that the retrieval condition leaves weights untouched by hashing every model tensor before and after the run. At each checkpoint, evaluate retention of earlier edits, new-edit success, paraphrase and multi-hop consistency, unrelated-prompt KL, WikiText-103 perplexity, MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC performance, latency, memory, retrieval failure rate, and robustness to irrelevant or conflicting retrieved records. Fit dose-response curves and test for monotonic or superlinear degradation while controlling for edit order and fact relatedness. Increasing forgetting or capability damage with edit count would support compounding harm; a stable parameter editor would refute that subclaim. If retrieval matches or exceeds editing on factual accuracy and ripple behavior while preserving baseline capabilities at acceptable latency and storage cost, it qualifies as a serious alternative rather than merely a fallback; poor retrieval robustness or prohibitive overhead would weaken that conclusion. Public sequential-edit checkpoints, tensor hashes, and matched retrieval logs could make replication of some conditions unnecessary, but independent evaluation would remain useful.

To address subclaims 1, 2, 5, and 6—whether parameter editing is reliable under realistic evaluation, whether prior near-perfect results survive, whether edits propagate globally, and whether damage compounds—run a preregistered sequential no-rollback benchmark using public COUNTERFACT and ZSRE data from Hugging Face. Apply ROME, MEMIT, MEND, unconstrained fine-tuning, and constrained fine-tuning to GPT-2 XL and GPT-J, retaining 1, 10, 100, and 1000 edits cumulatively; tune each method only on a disjoint validation split. At every checkpoint measure reliability on canonical edit prompts, generalization on paraphrases, COUNTERFACT ES/PS/NS, portability on subject-replacement, reversed, and one-hop probes, and locality on both relation-matched and random out-of-scope prompts. Measure global damage with output-distribution KL divergence, perplexity on WikiText-103, and accuracy on public HellaSwag, LAMBADA, Natural Questions, and an appropriate public MMLU release. Filter facts the base model cannot recall, validate generated prompts, report bootstrap confidence intervals, and compare cumulative editing with isolated rollback evaluation. Broadly distributed prediction changes or monotonic losses in locality and general capabilities as edit count rises—especially while canonical reliability remains high—would support the claim and explain why earlier headline scores were misleading. Stable reliability, paraphrase/portability performance, locality, perplexity, and downstream accuracy through large edit counts would refute or sharply qualify it; failure confined to one editor, dataset, layer, or backbone would indicate an incidental implementation issue rather than a general limitation. This experiment could be unnecessary if prior work released complete no-rollback trajectories, checkpoints, prompts, and downstream evaluations for the same cross-method and cross-backbone design, allowing independent reanalysis.

To address subclaims 3 and 4—whether the limitation is geometric and whether localized edits are amplified along low-variance representation directions—analyze the checkpoints and edits from the first experiment. For each edited layer and subject-token location, estimate the pre-edit activation covariance on a large public corpus such as WikiText-103, using held-out samples and shrinkage or randomized low-rank eigendecomposition. Decompose both the editor's weight update and its induced activation change into covariance-eigenvector bins, then calculate variance-normalized gain: the change in downstream hidden states, logits, and output KL per unit update norm for high-, middle-, and low-variance bins. Test global propagation on unrelated COUNTERFACT/ZSRE prompts and WikiText text by tracing each component through all later layers. Establish causality rather than correlation by applying norm-matched synthetic low-rank perturbations aligned with low-variance versus high-variance eigendirections, selecting magnitudes small enough to match the original edit's efficacy, and compare their downstream amplification and capability damage. Sweep layers, token positions, corruption magnitudes, and tracing aggregation rules; repeat localization with representation zeroing; and fit mixed-effects regressions predicting locality or downstream damage from inverse representation variance while controlling for layer, update norm, editor, relation, model, and edit count. Consistently larger gain and wider output changes for low-variance-aligned components, plus superior prediction of cumulative damage after controls, would support a geometric mechanism. Equal amplification across variance bins, disappearance under norm/layer controls, or dependence on one tracing procedure would reject or weaken that mechanism even if editing still fails empirically. This experiment could be replaced by released per-edit weight deltas, representative activation statistics, and downstream Jacobian or propagation measurements sufficient to reproduce the eigenspace analysis.

To address subclaims 7 and 8—whether a parameter-free approach leaves base weights untouched and is a serious alternative—compare IKE-style in-context editing and retrieval-backed external memory with ROME, MEMIT, MEND, and constrained fine-tuning on the same public COUNTERFACT, ZSRE, and, if available on Hugging Face, MQuAKE splits and the same GPT-2 XL/GPT-J backbones. Before and after every parameter-free edit, verify bitwise hashes of all base-model tensors, optimizer state, and model configuration; separately report any external index, stored demonstrations, or added module parameters so that 'weights untouched' is not confused with zero storage. Match methods by edit set and evaluate canonical reliability, paraphrase generalization, relation/subject portability, multi-hop propagation, out-of-scope locality, WikiText-103 perplexity, HellaSwag/LAMBADA/Natural Questions performance, latency, context-token cost, memory, and persistence across sessions. Run 1–1000 cumulative edits, include retrieval-disabled and irrelevant-memory controls, and evaluate both with and without the edited fact literally present in the final prompt to detect copying. A parameter-free method that preserves exact base-weight hashes and is Pareto-competitive in reliability, robust generalization, locality, accumulated damage, and practical resource cost would establish it as a serious alternative; success only through verbatim prompt insertion, severe context or latency costs, retrieval leakage, or poor portability would make it a limited fallback. If weight editors remain equally stable and substantially more accurate or efficient, the comparative claim would be refuted. This experiment could be unnecessary if existing studies provide auditable tensor hashes, external-storage accounting, matched sequential evaluations, and full quality-versus-resource Pareto results.
